quick.summary: How to handle conflicting data when multiple systems track the same thing.
quick.takeaway: Give every piece of data one clear owner to prevent conflicts.

beats.line: Marketing sees fifty active users. Billing sees forty. Which system is broken?
Maybe neither. Think of a busy kitchen with two chefs making soup.
If both keep adding salt when they feel like it, the soup is ruined.
So our systems are stepping on each other?
Yes. When multiple systems update the same user profile, they fight.
Because billing updates the address, and marketing updates the email?
Exactly. They both think they are right, and your data gets messy.
So we have two chefs salting the same soup.
How do we stop the fight?
To stop the fight, pick a system of record.
Can I just say the owner?
Sure. The owner is the one system allowed to change that data.
If marketing wants to update an address, they cannot do it themselves.
They have to ask the billing system to do it?
Yes. Billing owns the address. It updates it, then tells everyone else.
So marketing owns the email, and billing owns the address.
You got it. Every piece of data has exactly one owner.
And everyone else just reads it. No more salty soup.
Now your systems are working in harmony.

quiz.question: If the billing system owns the user address, what should the marketing system do if a user moves?
options: Send a request to billing to update the address.
Update the address in its own database secretly.
Override the billing system data at midnight.
quiz.explanation: Only the owner can update the data. Other systems must ask the owner to make the change.

quiz.question: To prevent errors, every system that uses customer data should be allowed to edit it.
quiz.explanation: If every system edits the data independently, you will end up with conflicting information.
